title: Square-factor saturation for the trilinear form xy+yz+zx
connection: OEIS A025052 studies positive integers omitted by xy+yz+zx; the page records Borwein–Choi's theorem that every N with a square factor is represented except 4 and 18. This shares F01/F08w/F13/F16w: a universal representation problem, algebraic exceptional strata, and a cubic/trilinear polynomial encoding.
why: The explicit parametrization by square-factor decomposition could suggest a way to make ES certificates from a repeated factor, distinct from residue covering.
first_step: Translate the A025052 square-factor parametrization to ES: fix n=m r² and test whether the induced denominators can be made positive integers; enumerate small m,r and record exactly where integrality fails.

title: Squarefree obstruction list for xy+yz+zx
connection: OEIS A055745 is the squarefree subset of integers not represented by xy+yz+zx, sharing F25/F08w/F13 and F04: a concrete finite-looking exceptional set arises within an algebraic family and representation counts are computable.
why: Comparing obstruction types rather than just the overall existence theorem may reveal whether ES failures cluster on squarefree or squareful inputs.
first_step: Compute ES failure counts separately for squarefree n and n with square factors over a modest prime range, and compare the apparent exceptional pattern with A055745's finite-list phenomenon.

title: Uniquely represented trilinear integers as a model for witness multiplicity
connection: OEIS A093669/A093670, cross-referenced by A025052, classify numbers with a unique representation by ab+ac+bc. They share F04/F13/F14: count integral points on a symmetric cubic-form fibre, including unusually sparse one-witness fibres.
why: ES work often needs a pointwise lower bound on representation counts; the neighboring exact-one locus is a useful benchmark for how divisor factorizations control multiplicity.
first_step: For primes p, compare the number of ordered ES solutions up to permutation with the analogous factorization count on a small trilinear surface; look for a divisor-sum identity or a stable multiplicity statistic.

title: Idoneal numbers and sparse failures of a cubic representation
connection: A025052 cross-references A000926 (Euler idoneal numbers) as integers not of the strict form ab+ac+bc with 0<a<b<c. This shares F08w/F13/F25/F31: a thin algebraically structured exceptional set tied to quadratic forms.
why: The quadratic-form reformulation offers a concrete bridge to ES's own quadratic-form/lattice perspectives, without assuming the obstruction mechanisms coincide.
first_step: Read the A000926 cross-reference and test whether the ES divisor-witness count on primes is better organized by discriminant/class data in Q(i) than by raw residue classes.

title: Goldbach's other conjecture and explicit finite exceptions
connection: OEIS A060003 records odd composites not expressible as a prime plus twice a square, with 5777 and 5993 identified as the known exceptions. It shares F01/F03/F25/F32: a universal arithmetic representation, finite explicit failures, and compact certificates checked by divisor/prime search.
why: This is a clean finite-exception analogue: the target's candidate witnesses can be enumerated cheaply and failure is unambiguous.
first_step: Build an ES analogue of A060003: for each prime p in increasing order, record the least denominator triple and the minimal search certificate; inspect whether witness-free candidates have a recognizable arithmetic signature.

title: Goldbach failure certificates versus ES certificate search
connection: The Goldbach-other problem turns a missing representation into a finite list of excluded prime-plus-square candidates. This matches F10/F21/F32/F25: divisor- or candidate-indexed witnesses, pointwise detection, short certificates, and explicit exceptions.
why: Its straightforward counterexample-certificate workflow is a useful blueprint for reproducible ES searches, even though it does not prove universal existence.
first_step: For each ES prime p, enumerate a single parameterized family of denominators and store a compact proof that all candidates in that family fail when none succeeds; compare against the full divisor criterion.

title: Schinzel's fixed-numerator three-unit-fraction generalization
connection: The MathOverflow question explicitly compares ES with Schinzel's conjecture that k/n is a sum of three unit fractions for fixed k and sufficiently large n. This shares F01w/F11/F12/F25: a numerator threshold, fixed-length Egyptian fractions, and a largest-exception function.
why: The dependence of the exceptional threshold n(k) may expose which parts of ES rely uniquely on numerator 4 rather than generic three-term decomposition.
first_step: Use the MO question's suggested n(k) viewpoint: compute largest failures for k=4,5,… over small ranges and test whether the same divisor-in-one-class parametrization extends uniformly in k.

title: Exceptional-set density question for Egyptian-fraction equations
connection: The MathOverflow discussion asks whether the set of failures to k/n=1/x+1/y+1/z has a power-saving bound under standard conjectures. This matches F05/F21/F22/F36: almost-all versus pointwise existence, thin exceptional sets, and limits of equidistribution heuristics.
why: The question isolates the gap between density control and eliminating the last exceptions, a central structural divide in ES.
first_step: Read the cited Elsholtz–Tao counting paper from the MO comment and identify which averaging step prevents its bound from implying a pointwise ES witness; test that precise step on prime moduli.

title: The largest exceptional denominator as a function of numerator
connection: For Schinzel's k/n variant, the MO question asks for the largest failure n(k), and notes a lower-growth bound. This shares F11/F12/F24/F25: numerator threshold, fixed number of unit fractions, heuristic finite exceptions, and explicit small failures.
why: A scaling law for n(k) could distinguish genuinely special features of 4/n from generic Egyptian-fraction existence.
first_step: For several small k, exhaustively find all n up to a modest cutoff with no three-term decomposition and plot the maximum against k; compare candidate growth to the stated k^(8/7) lower-bound direction before attempting proofs.

title: Egyptian fraction term-count threshold as a feature flip
connection: MO's Egyptian-fractions question distinguishes three terms from the easy four-term setting, matching F11/F12 while flipping the fixed-term threshold (three vs four). The useful feature flip is the sharpness of term count rather than the underlying rational input.
why: Understanding exactly why adding one term trivializes a family may identify which ES reductions must preserve the three-term constraint.
first_step: Fetch the related MO question on Egyptian fractions and compare its explicit four-term construction with the three-term k/n case; isolate the algebraic step that fails when one term is removed.

title: More-than-three unit fractions and numerator-dependent exceptions
connection: The MO question asks about k/n as a sum of a fixed number of unit fractions when k>4. This shares F01w/F11/F12/F25 and flips the exact numerator 4: fixed-term existence may become easier or harder with k.
why: A controlled numerator comparison can test whether ES's hard residue classes arise from a special small numerator or persist across nearby numerators.
first_step: On primes p in a small interval, compare the number of three-term representations of k/p for k=3,4,5 and tag each missing k against p's residue classes.

title: Four-term ES decompositions as a triviality control
connection: The MathOverflow question on ES with four terms supplies a direct neighboring problem where term count changes, matching F12/F11/F32 and flipping the conjectural three-term bound to four terms.
why: A four-term baseline can validate enumeration and expose whether a proposed three-term construction loses only one controlled denominator or relies on a genuinely deep coincidence.
first_step: Implement a canonical greedy four-term decomposition for 4/p, then compare its denominator scale and residues with the shortest three-term witnesses for the same primes.

title: Prime-minus-one characterization of a bilinear-form complement
connection: OEIS A005097 identifies the complement of values represented by 2xy+x+y as n with 2n+1 prime. This shares F01/F02/F10/F16w: an exact prime-indexed criterion, a simple polynomial representation, and a complementary exceptional set.
why: An exact arithmetic characterization of representability through a linear transform of n is a useful model for turning ES witness existence into a primality/divisor condition.
first_step: Rewrite the ES divisor certificate conditions as an equivalent primality or factorization test if possible; first search for an affine transform analogous to 2n+1 in the simple bilinear identity.

title: Bilinear polynomial representation via completing the product
connection: For A005097 the missing values are exactly those for which 2n+1 is prime, while represented values satisfy 2n+1=(2x+1)(2y+1) under the natural factorization. This shares F10/F15/F16w: a polynomial identity becomes a divisor-pair search on each fibre.
why: The simplest possible divisor-pair reduction mirrors the split-hyperbola ES slices and can suggest efficient certificate parameterizations.
first_step: Derive the analogous factorization on an ES fixed-variable slice and compare its residue constraints to the odd-factor pair factorization behind 2xy+x+y.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz proof on prime-sized cyclic seats
connection: A005097's comments describe Kohen's theorem: a prescribed-distance seating problem on 2n+1 positions is solvable for every distance list iff 2n+1 is prime, proved using Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. It shares F01/F03/F29/F31: universal finite-field conditions, prime residue structure, and an algebraic certificate.
why: This is a feature-flip: universality holds precisely on primes, rather than for every integer, and the proof is polynomial nonvanishing over a finite field.
first_step: Read Kohen's Nullstellensatz argument and test whether the polynomial coefficient-extraction method yields a nonzero count for ES witnesses modulo p, especially in the difficult p≡1 mod 4 class.

title: A prime criterion hidden in a missing-value sequence
connection: A005097 is simultaneously a prime transform and a complement of a polynomial value set. It shares F10/F16w/F24/F25: one can enumerate witnesses by factor pairs and the nonrepresented values have an exact, computable criterion.
why: It shows how an apparent open-ended omission problem can collapse to a sharp criterion; search for an analogous characterization of any ES subfamily's omitted primes.
first_step: Select a natural ES subfamily (e.g. one denominator divisible by p), calculate its omitted primes, and check whether omission is equivalent to primality of a low-degree transform.

title: Goldbach-other exceptions beyond the two famous composites
connection: A060003 records the full candidate list beginning 1,3,17,137,… and identifies 5777 and 5993 as its only known exceptions above the Stern-prime terms. It matches F01/F21/F25/F32: pointwise representation search, a rare exceptional set, and explicit negative certificates.
why: The difference between proven exceptions and a probable finite sequence is a useful discipline for ES computational claims and extrapolation.
first_step: For each claimed ES witness-free candidate, publish a terminating exact check over the full parameter range and separate proven failure from conjectural no-further-failures in the report.

title: Residue restriction on exceptional additive representations
connection: A060003 notes that its terms greater than 3 all lie in 6n−1. This shares F03/F25/F29: congruence restrictions sharply constrain the exceptional set, while leaving a sparse residue class to investigate.
why: The exceptional set's congruence compression is an inexpensive analogue of ES square-class residue analysis, and can guide targeted rather than blind searches.
first_step: Compute ES witness counts by residue class modulo 840 and by prime splitting in Q(i), then check whether any analogous single congruence class carries almost all low-count primes.

title: Stern primes and a second notion of additive nonrepresentation
connection: The A060003 comments identify several small exceptions as odd Stern primes, i.e. primes not of the form p+2b². This combines prime inputs with a restricted additive representation and finite exceptional values, matching F01p/F10/F25/F29.
why: Separating prime inputs from composite exceptions might reveal whether ES prime witnesses are governed by a different density or local obstruction than composite n.
first_step: Run the same candidate-generation code on ES primes and composites separately, comparing first-witness distributions and residue classes with the Stern-prime subset in A060003.

title: Large gaps between detected representations and exceptional candidates
connection: A060003 reports progressively improved lower bounds for the next possible omitted value, with no claim that the sequence is complete. This matches F23/F24/F25/F32: computation, heuristic finiteness, explicit exceptions, and verifiable search bounds.
why: Its cautious treatment of a finite-looking sequence is a model for how to use extensive ES computation without mistaking a cutoff for a theorem.
first_step: For ES, record the largest tested prime and the exact complete divisor-search bound alongside every ‘no counterexample’ statement; do not report a cutoff without the bound proof.

title: Square-factor theorem as a route from a thin stratum to near-universality
connection: A025052's Borwein–Choi result covers all N with a square factor except 4,18, leaving squarefree inputs as the difficult stratum. It shares F01/F05/F08w/F25 and is a feature-flip: broad coverage is proved off the squarefree locus.
why: This is a useful structural decomposition template: establish a broad algebraic subfamily first and isolate the genuinely hard inputs explicitly.
first_step: Partition ES primes and general n by square factors in the tied divisor quantities (4Cp+1 or p+4d), and test whether the certificate family handles all but a squarefree residual condition.

title: Explicit parametrization rather than mere existence for a cubic form
connection: A025052 gives explicit formulas for x,y,z after writing N=mn² and splitting according to n relative to m+1 and a residue k mod m+1. It matches F13/F15/F16w/F32: an integral surface is solved by casework and short parameters.
why: ES has many sufficient identities but comparatively less unified coverage; this suggests assembling a finite set of parameterized formulas with an explicit remainder case.
first_step: Adapt the three A025052 case splits as a design pattern for ES: choose an integer parameter, reduce to its residue modulo a linear function, and check whether the remainder becomes an integral positive third denominator.

title: Exceptional small values in a square-factor covering theorem
connection: The square-factor theorem for xy+yz+zx has the explicit exceptions 4 and 18. This shares F08w/F25/F27: a universal positivity-constrained representation has algebraic-family exceptions, and positivity matters to the theorem.
why: The exceptional small values may be artifacts of positivity or low-parameter degeneracy, distinctions also relevant to ES denominator positivity.
first_step: In ES parameter identities, list every boundary case where a denominator is zero, negative, or repeated; compare whether the remaining failures are similarly confined to low parameter values.

title: Quadratic-form reinterpretation of a trilinear omission set
connection: A025052 links its omission set to integers lacking an indecomposable positive definite binary quadratic form of the corresponding discriminant (as reported in the entry). This shares F13/F25/F31: a representation problem on a cubic form is reframed through quadratic forms and a sparse obstruction list.
why: An independent quadratic-form characterization may expose arithmetic invariants not visible in the original ES fractions.
first_step: Trace the Zhu–Shao/Peters reference from A025052 and check whether any discriminant/class-number invariant can be attached to ES's divisor witnesses in Q(i).

title: Squarefree tail bounds as a model for proving an omission list finite
connection: A055745 describes a finite-looking squarefree omission sequence for xy+yz+zx and cites Le's note on positive solutions. It matches F05/F08w/F25/F40: isolate a sparse algebraic locus, study its exceptional tail, and distinguish an observed finite list from a theorem.
why: The squarefree tail is the exact analogue of ES's concern with residual thin classes after easy congruence coverage.
first_step: Read Le's cited paper and extract any mechanism bounding squarefree nonrepresentables; test its divisor estimates on the squarefree parameters left after ES's 840-class identities.

title: Counting distinct unit-fraction solutions, not just proving existence
connection: MathOverflow 229514 asks for the number of strictly increasing tuples with reciprocal sum 1 and reports the unique 3-term solution 1/2+1/3+1/6. This shares F04/F12/F14/F21: an exact representation-count problem with symmetry removed and pointwise counts rather than existence alone.
why: A canonical count framework can clarify what ES's R(p) should count (ordered, unordered, or distinct denominators) and how symmetries affect estimates.
first_step: Adopt the increasing-denominator convention from the MO question and recompute small-prime ES representation counts, comparing them to ordered counts after dividing by S3 orbit sizes.

title: Odd-denominator restriction creates exact term-count obstructions
connection: The accepted answer on MO 229514 reports the distinct odd-denominator equation sum 1/x_i=1 has no solutions for even term count, and five solutions at the first odd case n=9. This shares F11/F12/F25/F27: a term-count threshold and positivity/integrality constraints create sharp exceptions.
why: It is a controlled example where imposing a denominator congruence condition radically changes existence, akin to ES's residue-class-sensitive witness families.
first_step: For ES, classify triples by denominator parity pattern and test whether excluding one pattern leaves an exceptional family analogous to the even-term impossibility.

title: Landau-style bounds on the number of reciprocal representations
connection: The MO answer to 229514 cites Landau's bound for solutions to sum 1/x_i=1 with unrestricted positive integer denominators. This shares F04/F12/F21/F32: bounded-length unit fractions, representation multiplicity, and an explicit counting bound.
why: Even a crude universal upper bound can benchmark ES witness-count heuristics and help distinguish genuine polylog behavior from counting conventions.
first_step: Follow the Landau reference identified in the MO answer and see whether its argument, applied to 4/p after scaling, yields any nontrivial upper bound on R(p).

title: Odd unit-fraction solution counts and polynomial lower bounds
connection: The same MO answer cites a result giving a lower bound on the number of odd-denominator solutions for larger odd term counts, while exact counts remain unknown. This matches F04w/F12/F21/F22: a lower-bound count for constrained reciprocal representations but a gap to exact pointwise behavior.
why: The proof's construction of many solutions under a congruence restriction may transfer to lower bounds for ES representations in selected residue classes.
first_step: Read Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang, cited in the answer (arXiv:1108.6118), and extract its solution-generating operation; test whether it produces multiplicative families of ES triples.

title: Group class equations naturally generate reciprocal sums
connection: MO 229514 notes that a finite group with n conjugacy classes gives a reciprocal sum equal to 1 using centralizer orders. This shares F01/F12/F14/F33: a structured family of unit-fraction representations arises from a symmetry object and its orbit stabilizers.
why: Although centralizer denominators are usually repeated, the orbit-stabilizer construction offers a structural source of identities and a possible way to build ES certificates from group actions.
first_step: Check whether any finite-group class equation can be normalized to 4/p with three distinct centralizer orders; start with small groups and inspect the resulting divisibility constraints.

title: Denominator-sum generating sequence for reciprocal representations
connection: The MO answer points to OEIS A051907, counting representations of 1 as unit fractions with a fixed denominator sum. This shares F04/F12/F19/F21: a coefficient/counting viewpoint turns reciprocal solutions into sequence coefficients indexed by a complexity statistic.
why: Generating-function and dynamic-programming methods can offer an independent way to enumerate restricted ES witnesses and compare expected counts.
first_step: Inspect A051907's definition and recurrence, then formulate the corresponding generating series for ordered ES triples by denominator sum or maximum denominator and compare low coefficients.

title: Strictly ordered cubic-form representations and symmetry reduction
connection: OEIS A093669 counts unique representations by ab+ac+bc under 0<a<b<c, removing permutation symmetry. It shares F04/F13/F14: a symmetric three-variable surface whose raw point count is converted to canonical unordered witnesses.
why: ES's S3 symmetry creates overcounting; the ordered-triple convention in this sequence offers an exact and transparent normalization.
first_step: For primes p, count only x≤y≤z ES triples and compare with the fully ordered count, separately tracking repeated-coordinate strata.

title: Unique-representation locus as a low-multiplicity test
connection: A093669 lists integers with exactly one strictly ordered representation as ab+ac+bc, sharing F04/F13/F25 and contrasting ES's expected polylogarithmic abundance with a rigid one-point fibre.
why: A unique-witness locus is a sensitive place to test whether an ES construction proves mere existence or can force multiple genuinely distinct solution orbits.
first_step: Enumerate ES primes with exactly one unordered solution orbit up to a modest cutoff and compare their factorization and residue signatures to the one-representation trilinear terms.

title: Boundary-inclusive representation count changes the exceptional set
connection: A093670 counts unique ab+ac+bc representations with 1≤a≤b≤c, unlike A093669's strict inequalities. It shares F13/F14/F25 and flips the boundary convention, showing that allowing coincident coordinates changes which values have a unique witness.
why: ES parametrizations often rely on distinctness assumptions only for convenience; tracking boundary strata separately can expose missed or degenerate certificates.
first_step: Split ES solutions into all-distinct, exactly-two-equal, and all-equal denominator triples and verify whether any attempted reduction discards a necessary boundary stratum.

title: Factor-pair enumeration for a unique cubic-form witness
connection: A093669 provides a computation for unique ab+ac+bc representations by looping over a,b and testing whether n−ab is divisible by a+b, yielding c. This matches F10/F15/F32: each fibre is reduced to a divisor/congruence test and can be exhaustively certified.
why: It is a low-cost exact enumeration architecture analogous to fixed-variable ES hyperbola factorization, and can validate a new ES candidate-family search.
first_step: Implement the A093669 loop pattern for ES after fixing one denominator, using the exact split-hyperbola divisor condition; compare outputs against independent brute force for small p.

title: Squarefree tail bounds as a model for proving an omission list finite
connection: A055745 describes a finite-looking squarefree omission sequence for xy+yz+zx and cites Le's note on positive solutions. It matches F05/F08w/F25/F40: isolate a sparse algebraic locus, study its exceptional tail, and distinguish an observed finite list from a theorem.
why: The squarefree tail is the exact analogue of ES's concern with residual thin classes after easy congruence coverage.
first_step: Read Le's cited paper and extract any mechanism bounding squarefree nonrepresentables; test its divisor estimates on the squarefree parameters left after ES's 840-class identities.
